title: Optimal Tradeoffs for Estimating Pauli Observables
authors: Sitan Chen (Harvard University, USA), Weiyuan Gong (Harvard University, USA), Qi Ye (Tsinghua Unversity, China)
abstract: We revisit the problem of Pauli shadow tomography: given copies of an unknown $n$-qubit quantum state $\rho$, estimate $\Tr(P\rho)$ for some set of Pauli operators $P$ to within additive error $\epsilon$. This has been a popular testbed for exploring the advantage of protocols with quantum memory over those without: with enough memory to measure two copies at a time, one can use Bell sampling to estimate $|\Tr(P\rho)|$ for all $P$ using $O(n/\epsilon^4)$ copies, but with $k\le n$ qubits of memory, $\Omega(2^{(n-k)/3})$ copies are needed. These results leave open several natural questions. How does this picture change in the physically relevant setting where one only needs to estimate a certain \emph{subset} of Paulis? What is the optimal dependence on $\epsilon$? What is the optimal tradeoff between quantum memory and sample complexity? We answer all of these questions: For any subset $A$ of Paulis and any family of measurement strategies, we completely characterize the optimal sample complexity, up to $\log |A|$ factors. We show any protocol that makes $\poly(n)$-copy measurements must make $\Omega(1/\epsilon^4)$ measurements. For any protocol that makes $\poly(n)$-copy measurements and only has $k < n$ qubits of memory, we show that $\widetilde{\Theta}(\min\{2^n/\epsilon^2, 2^{n-k}/\epsilon^4\})$ copies are necessary and sufficient. The protocols we propose can also estimate the actual values $\Tr(P\rho)$, rather than just their absolute values as in prior work. Additionally, as a byproduct of our techniques, we establish tight bounds for the task of purity testing and show that it exhibits an intriguing phase transition not present in the memory-sample tradeoff for Pauli shadow tomography.

Our starting point is a recurring shortcoming with existing
sample complexity lower bounds for bounded-memory protocols [19], [21], [29], namely that they all lose a factor of 3
in the exponent. This stems from a specific technical reason:
these arguments all rely on arguing that after one measurement
of ρ sampled from either ensemble, the quantum memory does
not differ too much in trace distance under either ensemble,
in expectation over P . In the language of our work, this can
be thought of as a bound on a certain matrix-valued version
of the δc,M quantity in Eq. (1) (see e.g. Eq. (133) in [21]).
Unfortunately, it is unclear how to optimally “chain together”
bounds in expectation for this matrix term; that is, given that
little information is gained in expectation from one round of
the protocol, at least as measured by this matrix term, how
do we argue that little information is gained over multiple
rounds? For this, the aforementioned works resort to a certain
lossy pruning argument, and this is where they lose the factor
of 3. In contrast, we eschew such an argument by identifying
a clean scalar-valued quantity δc,M that correctly quantifies
the amount of information gained in a single measurement,
and which can be chained together in a lossless fashion
via a martingale analysis like in [22], [25]. The minimax
problem in Theorem 1 falls out quite naturally from this proof
technique, and we defer the details to Section VI.

Theorem 7. The sample complexity of purity testing for
protocols that make 2-copy measurements and have k qubits
of quantum memory is Θ(min{2n−k , 2n/2 }).
Both upper and lower bounds in Theorem 7 are new. Interestingly, our result implies that with k ≤ n/2 qubits of quantum
memory, no protocol can improve upon the sample complexity
achieved by protocols with no quantum memory. This is in
stark contrast to Pauli shadow tomography where, at least for
ϵ = Θ(1), the sample complexity continuously improves as k
increases from 0 to n. Instead, the memory-sample tradeoff
for purity testing exhibits a “second-order phase transition” at
k = n/2 (see Figure 1).
III. OVERVIEW OF TECHNIQUES
Here, we provide a high-level discussion of the techniques
for all theorems mentioned so far. The detailed proof can be
found in the full version of this paper [24].
a) Minimax lower bound.: Our lower bounds for Pauli
shadow tomography throughout this paper exploit the “learning tree” framework introduced in [4], [16], [21]–[23], [51].
Roughly speaking, in this approach one models the learning
protocol as a decision tree, and any choice of unknown state ρ
will induce a distribution on the leaves. The goal is to define a
pair of ensembles of ρ such that the resulting leaf distributions
are statistically indistinguishable unless the tree is sufficiently
